t: Count Distinct Numbers on Board — Converging Simulation
o: Start with n on the board; each day, for every board number x, every i in [1,n] with x % i == 1 gets added. After a billion days, count distinct numbers. For n=5 the board grows 5 -> {5,2,4} -> {5,2,4,3}, giving 4. Key observation: if x is on the board and x >= 2, then x % (x-1) == 1, so x-1 gets added. Hence from n we successively obtain n-1, n-2, ..., 2. The answer is therefore n-1 for n > 1, and 1 for n = 1.
k: x % (x-1) == 1 for all x >= 2, so every board number immediately spawns its predecessor.
Once 2 appears, nothing new beyond 2..n can appear (all i considered are <= n, and only i in [2,n] can satisfy x % i == 1 with x <= n).

a.i: By the predecessor argument the board stabilizes at exactly {2, 3, ..., n} (plus n itself), so the answer is n-1 unless n = 1, when only 1 is ever on the board.

c.javascript: var distinctIntegers = function(n) { return n === 1 ? 1 : n - 1; };

a.i: Directly simulate days until the board stops changing. Since the board gains at least its maximum element minus one each phase, it converges within n days; each day costs O(n^2) checks, giving O(n^3) worst case — fine for n <= 100 and a good sanity check of the formula.
s: Repeat: for each x in the set, add every i in [1,n] with x % i == 1; stop when nothing changes.
a.t: O(n^3) worst case across all simulated days — trivially fast for n <= 100.

w: State the x % (x-1) == 1 observation first; it makes the O(1) answer rigorous. Pitfall: mis-handling n = 1 (answer 1, not 0). Follow-up: what if the daily rule were x % i == 0, or i ranged over unbounded integers?
